1-2.title: Transformations of Functions
1-2.status: Draft, Tue Oct 6 2026, from the Sep 27 packet plan (Examples 1-5, focus Ex 5, Try It 5 graded, Ex 6 dropped); PLC has not re-cut this packet yet

objectives.learning: I can tell which transformations (left/right, up/down, stretch, reflection) turn a parent graph into a new graph.
objectives.language: I can describe a transformation in writing using the words left, right, up, down, stretch, compress and reflect.
objectives.essentialQuestion: How do the values a, b, h and k in a·f(b(x − h)) + k move or reshape the graph of f?

quizFocus.source: aga_24_a2_na_0102_lq.pdf; the only 1-2 item carried into the Topic 1 assessment (end of October)
quizFocus.what: Select all the transformations of f(x) = x^2 that produce the graph of g (downward parabola, vertex (-1, -2)). Choices: A 1 left, B 1 right, C 2 down, D horizontal stretch by 2, E vertical stretch by 2, F reflection across the x-axis.
quizFocus.answer: A, C, D, F (TE key): 1 left, 2 down, horizontal stretch by 2, reflect across the x-axis. g(x) = -(1/2 (x+1))^2 - 2.
needs: read the vertex and use the sign rule: (x + 1) is 1 LEFT, -2 is 2 down (Example 1, IXL F6J)
opens down = reflection across the x-axis (Example 2, IXL PHV)
wider than x^2 = horizontal stretch, not vertical stretch; check a point one unit from the vertex (Example 3, IXL NNY)
put it together from the graph with no equation given (Example 5, IXL KT8 / R7X)

examples.title: Translate a function
examples.why: Left/right and up/down; the sign trap in (x + 1) is half of quiz item 1.

examples.title: Reflect a function across the x- or y-axis
examples.why: Opens-down = reflection across the x-axis (choice F).

examples.title: Understand stretches and compressions
examples.why: Horizontal vs vertical stretch (choice D vs E); the hardest distinction on the item.

dok3.label: Practice & Problem Solving 17, Error Analysis (Example 5 DOK 3; item 37 is the SAT/ACT alternative)
dok3.task: Monisha compares f(x) = |x| and g(x) = |2x - 4|. She says g is f translated 4 right and compressed horizontally by 2. What is her error?
dok3.key: |2x - 4| = 2|x - 2|, so g is f translated 2 right and stretched vertically by 2 (or, read as f(2(x - 2)), compressed horizontally by 1/2 and shifted 2 right).
dok3.why: Students must factor inside the absolute value before reading the transformations; the same inside-vs-outside reasoning as quiz item 1's choice D vs E.

modelDiscuss.source: 2024 TE, Step 1 Explore (this lesson's opener is Explore & Reason, powered by Desmos)
modelDiscuss.situation: The graph of f(x) = |x| is shown. Students graph g(x) = |x + c| for several values of c from -5 to 5.
studentPrompts: A. Graph g(x) = |x + c| several times with different values of c (any value from -5 to 5).
B. Look for Relationships: predict what happens to the graph if c is greater than 100. What if c is between 0 and 1/2? (Very large shift left; very small shift left.)

teQuestions.q: What does the graph tell you about the range of f(x) = |x|?
teQuestions.a: The range is greater than or equal to zero.

teQuestions.q: What can you predict about the range of g(x) = |x + c| for different values of c?
teQuestions.a: Whatever c is, the range is still greater than or equal to zero.

teQuestions.q: How can you find points to graph for each function?
teQuestions.a: Make a table of values for x from -5 to 5 and compute y.

teQuestions.q: What do you notice about the vertex of each function?
teQuestions.a: The vertices all lie on the x-axis.

teQuestions.q: How does the graph change if the coefficient of f(x + c) is negative? Graph -f(x + c) for three of your functions.
teQuestions.a: The graphs of -f(x + c) are reflections of f(x + c) across the x-axis.

teQuestions.q: If f(x) has a horizontal shift, what part of the function has been changed?
teQuestions.a: x stands for the domain, so the operation is applied to x inside the parentheses.

teQuestions.q: If f(x) has a vertical shift, what part of the function has been changed?
teQuestions.a: f(x) stands for the range, so the operation is applied to f(x).

teQuestions.q: What happens to the graph if c is a negative number?
teQuestions.a: The graph shifts to the right when c is negative.

modelDiscuss.caution: The After questions are the moment to introduce a·f(b(x - h)) + k. The Mon/Tue whiteboard table activity (a2_1-2_plan_oct5-7) already does part A on paper; the TE's 'table of values' answer matches it.

objectives.language: I can explain, in writing, which rule applies on each part of the domain, using the words piece, interval, open circle and closed circle.
objectives.essentialQuestion: How do you model a situation where different rules apply to different parts of the domain?

quizFocus.source: aga_24_a2_na_0103_lq.pdf
quizFocus.what: Which rule defines the function in the graph? Two linear pieces; the four choices differ by the slope of the right piece (-3x+9 vs x-3) and by the endpoint inequalities (< vs <=).
quizFocus.answer: B: x-1 if -3 <= x < 1; -3x+9 if 2 <= x <= 4 (read from the graph; verify against the TE key)
needs: slope of each piece from two points (IXL W67)
open circle = strict inequality, closed dot = inclusive (whiteboard drill)

items.3: Write the function for a V graph (vertex (6,0), slopes -5 and 5) as two linear pieces in the form a(x+b): Example 3 skill; Example 4 (absolute value as piecewise) is an optional shortcut, not needed.
items.4: Graph the admission-price step function from a table: Example 5.
items.5: Domain and range of the step function in item 4: Example 5 (the fast packet already asks for domain and range).

modelDiscuss.situation: A music teacher buys guitar strings. Store A sells a single pack for $6; Store B sells a bundle of 4 packs for $20.
studentPrompts: A. Make graphs that show the income each store receives if the teacher needs 1-20 packs.
B. Describe the shape of each store's graph. Why are the graphs different?
C. Communicate Precisely: for what numbers of strings is it cheaper to buy from Store B? Explain how you know. (4, 7, 8, 11, 12, 14-20)

teQuestions.q: How do stores A and B compare?
teQuestions.a: Store A sells strings individually; Store B sells them in packages of 4.

teQuestions.q: How do the stores' graphs represent the cost of the guitar strings?
teQuestions.a: Store A rises steadily, $6 more per string. Store B is constant at $20 for 1-4 strings, then jumps $20 and is constant again.

teQuestions.q: How can you represent the stores' prices as equations?
teQuestions.a: Store A: y = 6x. Store B: y = 20 for 0 < x <= 4, 40 for 4 < x <= 8, 60 for 8 < x <= 12, 80 for 12 < x <= 16, 100 for 16 < x <= 20.

teQuestions.q: What is different about the shapes of the two graphs?
teQuestions.a: Graph A is linear; graph B is a set of horizontal segments (a step function).

teQuestions.q: Why do you use dots rather than line segments to graph these two functions?
teQuestions.a: Dots show whole numbers of strings only; you cannot buy a fraction of a string.

modelDiscuss.caution: The opener is a step-function situation (Example 5 content, cut). It still works as the hook; only the early-finishers equations question leads toward Example 3.

objectives.learning: I can write an arithmetic sequence with a recursive definition and with an explicit definition, and translate from one to the other.
objectives.language: I can explain how a recursive definition and an explicit definition describe the same sequence, using the words first term, common difference, previous term, and term number.
objectives.essentialQuestion: What is an arithmetic sequence, and how do you represent and find its terms and their sums?

quizFocus.source: a2_1-4_TE.tex Lesson Quiz (TE printed page 39A); aga_24_a2_na_0104_lq.pdf (downloaded; its five items match the TE word for word). Short form a2_1-4_quiz_fast.pdf carries Savvas items 1, 3, 4 under their Savvas numbers; items 2 and 5 are on the full Savvas quiz only. Topic 1 Assessment (TE printed page 57A-57B, Topic_01_Teacher_Edition.pdf PDF pages 91-92) items 7-10 are 1-4: 7 recursive formula from a context (Enzo's profit 900, 500, ..., -300; a1 = 900, d = -400; DOK 3), 8 explicit from a given recursive formula and use it for round 7 (a_n = 2 + 7(n - 1), 44 prizes; DOK 2), 9 series sum in context with n unknown (drone 11, 22, ..., 77 m; 308 m; DOK 2), 10 reasonable domain (theater, 10 rows; integers 1 through 10; DOK 2).
quizFocus.what: Item 3: a bucket holds 100 potatoes; Hal removes and cleans 4 per minute. Choose the explicit definition for the potatoes left after n minutes: A a_n = 4 - 100(n - 1); B a_n = 100 - 4(n - 1); C a_n = 96 + 4(n - 1); D a_n = 96 - 4(n - 1). Item 4: complete the recursive definition f(n) = {[ ], n = 1; f(n - 1) + [ ], n > 1} for Gabriela's birthday deposits ($50 the first birthday, each deposit $25 more than the one before).
quizFocus.answer: Item 3: D, a_n = 96 - 4(n - 1) (after 1 minute 96 are left, so a1 = 96, d = -4; distractor B counts from 0 minutes). Item 4: 50; 25. Verify against the TE key on quiz day.
needs: common difference: the constant difference between consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence (vocabulary box)
the explicit form a_n = a1 + d(n - 1): the number multiplying (n - 1) is d (Example 3A; IXL H82)
the recursive form: a1, then a_n = a_(n-1) + d for n > 1 (Example 3B; IXL ZAH)
read a1 and d from a word problem, and notice when term 1 is 'after 1 minute' rather than the starting amount (packet Practice a, the structural parallel of item 3)
d is negative when the amount goes down by the same amount each time (item 1 bonus; IXL C8R)
for the Topic 1 Assessment: a reasonable domain is the term numbers that make sense, integers 1 through the last term (packet Practice a, last line)

dok3.task: Felipe and Gregory are given the arithmetic sequence -1, 6, 13, .... Gregory wrote the explicit definition a_n = -1 + 7(n - 1) for the sequence. Felipe wrote the definition as a_n = 7n - 8. Which one of them is correct? Explain.

modelDiscuss.source: 2024 TE page 31B (Step 1; this lesson's opener is Critique & Explain)
modelDiscuss.situation: Yumiko and Hugo look at a table of the number of families attending a party (0, 1, 2, 3, 4) and the items needed to fill pinatas (1, 5, 9, 13, 17). Yumiko writes f(1) = 1 + 4 = 5, f(2) = f(1) + 4 = 9, f(3) = f(2) + 4 = 13, f(4) = f(3) + 4 = 17. Hugo writes g(x) = 1 + 4x.
studentPrompts: A. Describe the pattern Yumiko found for finding items needed for the pinatas. (Each number is 4 more than the previous number.)
B. Describe the pattern Hugo found for finding items needed for the pinatas. (He used a formula to calculate the number of items.)

C. Use Structure: compare the two methods. Which method would be more useful in finding the items needed when 100 family members attend? Why? (Hugo's: g(100) directly; Yumiko's needs f(1) through f(99) first.)

teQuestions.q: What do you notice about the values in the table?
teQuestions.a: The input values increase by 1. The output values increase by 4.

teQuestions.q: How else could you represent the data in the table?
teQuestions.a: You could plot the ordered pairs of inputs and outputs on a coordinate plane.

teQuestions.q: Plot the ordered pairs on a coordinate plane. Draw a line to connect all the points. What do you notice?
teQuestions.a: All the points lie on a line. The equation of the line is the same as the equation Hugo found.

teQuestions.q: Consider the ordered pairs (0,3), (1,5), (2,7), (3,9), (4,11). Describe two different methods for finding the outputs. Compare your methods.
teQuestions.a: Use a graph: as x increases by 1, y increases by 2. Or find an equation, for example f(x) = 2x + 3.

teQuestions.q: What differences do you notice between Yumiko's and Hugo's methods?
teQuestions.a: In Yumiko's method you need the previous value to calculate the current value. In Hugo's method you can calculate the current value directly.

teQuestions.q: Find the average rate of change between a few pairs of points. What can you conclude about the function represented in the table?
teQuestions.a: The average rate of change is always 4, so these values are probably from a linear function.

modelDiscuss.caution: The opener is Example 3 in disguise: Yumiko's rule is recursive (previous term), Hugo's is explicit (term number); name them that way in the After question. Hugo's g(x) = 1 + 4x starts at 0 attendees, while a sequence starts at n = 1, so a_n = a1 + d(n - 1) gives a different-looking formula depending on whether term 1 is 0 or 1 attendee. Settle it on the board: it is the same trap as quiz item 3 (100 potatoes, but a1 = 96 after 1 minute). The TE's question C says 'family members' while the table counts families.

1-5.title: Solving Equations and Inequalities by Graphing

objectives.learning: I can solve an equation or inequality by graphing both sides and reading where the graphs meet.
objectives.language: I can say "the solution is where the graphs intersect" and "the inequality is true where one graph is above (or below) the other."
objectives.essentialQuestion: How can you solve an equation or inequality by graphing?

quizFocus.source: aga_24_a2_na_0105_lq.pdf, items 1-2 (sketch the graph, then pick the solution). Topic 1 assessment item 11 (TE printed page 57A-57B, Topic_01_Teacher_Edition.pdf PDF pages 91-92; DOK 2, skill A56) is the ONLY 1-5 item on the Nov 9-10 assessment, and it is this same task with the graph already drawn: Form A 'Use the graph to solve |x+3| - 1 = (x+2)^2' (x = -2, x = -1); Form B '(1/2)|x+1| + 1 = |x|' (key reads x = -1, x = -3, but the graph and the algebra give x = -1 and x = 3; check before using Form B). Inequalities by graphing (items 3-4) and tables (item 5) are not on the topic assessment. Proposal: for this quiz count items 1 and 2 as the graded 20 (sketch 10, solution 10) and make item 4 the +5 bonus; the Sep 28 'Q3 + Q4' rule was written for 1-1 and 1-2, not for every quiz.
quizFocus.what: Item 1: sketch a graph you could use to solve -2|x-1| + 3 = (2/5)x - 11/5 (grid -4..4). Item 2: the solution, choices A x = 1; B x = -2; C x = -2, x = 3; D x = -2, x = 1, x = 3. Topic assessment item 11 is the same skill with the two graphs given: read the x-coordinates of both crossings.
quizFocus.answer: Item 1: downward V with vertex (1, 3) and the line through (0, -11/5) with slope 2/5; crossings at (-2, -3) and (3, -1). Item 2: C (checked algebraically: x >= 1 gives -2.4x = -7.2, x = 3; x < 1 gives 1.6x = -3.2, x = -2). Distractor A is the vertex's x; distractor D adds the vertex to the crossings. Verify against the TE key on quiz day.

dok3.label: Practice & Problem Solving 7, Higher Order Thinking (Example 1 DOK 3; items 32 and 35 are the Example 2 DOK 3 alternatives)
dok3.task: Sadie used a graph to solve an equation. The graph shows the line y = 2x + 3 and the downward V y = -|x+1| - 1 crossing at (-3, -3). What equation did Sadie solve? Explain how to verify your equation is correct.
dok3.key: 2x + 3 = -|x+1| - 1; the solution is x = -3. Verify by substituting: 2(-3) + 3 = -|-3+1| - 1 gives -3 = -3.
dok3.why: Reverses quiz items 1-2 and Topic 1 assessment item 11 (graph to equation instead of equation to graph) with no technology, and the verification step is the MP.3 argument the Topic 1 assessment never asks for (its two DOK 3 items, 7 and 14, are arithmetic sequences and a system). modelDiscuss.situation: A homeowner has 32 feet of fencing to build three sides of a rectangular chicken run (the house is the fourth side).
studentPrompts: A. Make a table of values for the length, width, and area of different rectangular runs that use 32 feet of fencing. Then write a function for the area in terms of the width. (A(x) = x(32 - x)/2)
B. Graph your function. (Downward parabola through (0,0), (16,128), (32,0).)
C. Reason: explain what happens where the graph intersects the x-axis. (One dimension is 0, so the area is 0.)

teQuestions.q: What are the formulas for the perimeter and area of a rectangle?
teQuestions.a: Perimeter = 2w + 2l; Area = lw.

teQuestions.q: How does the perimeter of the chicken run help you discover the area?
teQuestions.a: Fencing covers three sides, so w + 2l = 32 and l = (32 - w)/2. The area is w(32 - w)/2.

teQuestions.q: Write and graph a function for the area if the perimeter is 44 ft. List three possible values for the length, width and area.
teQuestions.a: f(x) = x(44 - x)/2 (the TE prints (44 - x)/2 and drops the width factor). Check students' graphs and values.

teQuestions.q: How can the graph help you solve A(x) = 0?
teQuestions.a: The x-intercepts are where A(x) = 0, so they are the solutions.

teQuestions.q: How can you use the graph to calculate the length?
teQuestions.a: The x-coordinate is the width; the length is 16 minus half the width.

teQuestions.when: Habits of Mind, Make Sense and Persevere
teQuestions.q: For what widths will the area be at least 110 square feet?
teQuestions.a: 10 <= x <= 22 (read where the parabola is at or above y = 110).

modelDiscuss.caution: The opener is a quadratic area model, not a linear one; use the Habits of Mind question (area at least 110) as the bridge, because it is Example 2A in disguise: draw y = 110 and read where the parabola is above it. Do not let the table-building in part A eat the period; two or three rows and the function are enough.

modelDiscuss.situation: The graph shows two lines that intersect at one point (a blue line through (0, 3) and a steeper red line; the TE's early-finisher answer gives them as y = 0.5x + 3 and y = 3x - 5, which meet exactly at (3.2, 4.6)).
studentPrompts: A. What are the approximate coordinates of the point of intersection? (TE sample: (3.1, 4.8))

B. How could you verify whether the coordinates you estimated are, in fact, the solution? Is the point the solution to the equations of both lines? (Substitute into the equation of each line; yes, the intersection is the solution.)

C. Make Sense and Persevere: use your result to refine your approximation, and try again. Can you find the point of intersection this way? Is there a more efficient way? (Yes, as long as the coordinates are rational; solving algebraically might be more efficient.)

teQuestions.q: What do you notice about the graph?
teQuestions.a: There are two linear functions. They both have positive slopes and intersect at approximately (3, 4.5).

teQuestions.q: What do the coordinates of the point of intersection of the two lines represent?
teQuestions.a: The point is a solution to the equations of both lines. If you input the x-coordinate into both functions, the output, the y-coordinate, will be the same.

teQuestions.q: What is the equation in slope-intercept form for each line?
What do you notice about the point of intersection?
teQuestions.a: The point lies on both lines. The point is a solution to the equation of each line. There is only one point of intersection.

teQuestions.q: How many possible points of intersection can two straight lines have?
teQuestions.a: Two straight lines can intersect once. Two straight lines that are parallel will never intersect. Two straight lines that are the same line will intersect at every point.

teQuestions.q: The graphs of two equations appear to intersect at the point (2, 3). Does that guarantee that x = 2 and y = 3 is a solution to both equations? Explain.
teQuestions.a: No; graphing shows an approximate solution. To show that the point is the exact solution, substitute x = 2 and y = 3 into the original equations.

modelDiscuss.caution: Fits the kept Example 1: estimate from the graph, then check. The TE's estimates disagree ((3, 4.5), (3.1, 4.8); the early-finisher lines meet at (3.2, 4.6)), so accept close estimates; part C shows why the exact pair needs algebra. modelDiscuss.source: 2024 TE page 61B, Step 1 Explore (Explore & Reason, powered by Desmos)
modelDiscuss.situation: A table gives A(x), the area of a square as a function of side length x units (x a positive real number): x = 1, 2, 3, 4 gives A(x) = 1, 4, 9, 16.
studentPrompts: A. Consider the function where the areas in the table are doubled. Write the equation of a function that represents this. (f(x) = 2(x^2))

B. Look for Relationships: graph the ordered pairs for both A(x) and your new function. How would you describe the differences in the locations of these points? (The new points are closer to the y-axis; each y-value is twice that of A(x).)
C. Find the equation for a function whose x-values are the same as A(x) but whose y-values are 2 units greater than each y-value in A(x). (g(x) = x^2 + 2)

teQuestions.q: Do you see any patterns in the table?
teQuestions.a: The value of A(x) in the third row is equal to the square of the value of x in the first row.

teQuestions.q: Why is it helpful to think of the new function described in Part A in terms of A(x)?
teQuestions.a: You know that A(x) = x^2. The new function is 2x^2, so f(x) = 2A(x): if you know A(x), multiply it by 2.

teQuestions.q: What does A(x) + 2 mean in relation to A(x)?
teQuestions.a: Find the value of A(x), and then add 2 to that value.

teQuestions.q: Suppose you double both the length and the width of the square to make a larger square. How are the corresponding areas affected?
teQuestions.a: The corresponding areas are 4 times as great.

teQuestions.q: What strategy can you use to determine the relationship between the new function described in Part A and A(x)?
teQuestions.a: Add another row to the table for the values of f(x). Each value of f(x) is twice the value of A(x), so f(x) = 2A(x).

teQuestions.q: What strategy can you use to determine the value of f(x) + 1 if you know the value of A(x)?
teQuestions.a: Multiply the value of A(x) by 2 and then add 1.

teQuestions.q: Suppose you started with a different function. Would altering A(x) in the two ways you did have the same effect?
teQuestions.a: Yes; multiplying any function by 2 doubles each y-value, and adding 2 raises each y-value by 2.

modelDiscuss.caution: The opener only stretches (a) and shifts up (k); it never moves the vertex sideways, so it sets up Example 1 (cut) more than the kept Examples. Use Part C as the bridge to Example 2: g(x) = x^2 + 2 has vertex (0, 2), so k is the y-coordinate of the vertex; then ask where the vertex would be for (x - 3)^2 + 2. Keep it to two table rows and Part C; Part B's plotting can eat the period.

modelDiscuss.situation: Jordan and Emery are rewriting the vertex form of the quadratic function y = 2(x - 4)^2 + 5 in the form y = ax^2 + bx + c. Jordan: = (2x - 8)^2 + 5 = 4x^2 - 32x + 64 + 5 = 4x^2 - 32x + 69. Emery: = 2(x^2 - 16) + 5 = 2x^2 - 32 + 5 = 2x^2 - 27.
studentPrompts: A. Communicate Precisely: Did Jordan rewrite the equation correctly? Did Emery? Explain. (Neither; the correct equation is y = 2x^2 - 16x + 37.)

B. Without rewriting the equation, how could you prove that Jordan or Emery's equations are not equivalent to the original? (Neither squared the binomial correctly: Jordan distributed the 2 before squaring; Emery did not square the binomial correctly.)

teQuestions.q: How was the process used by Jordan similar to that used by Emery? How was it different?
teQuestions.a: Both students expanded the binomial. Jordan distributed the coefficient before expanding, while Emery used an incorrect sign and forgot to include the middle term.

teQuestions.q: How does understanding the order of operations help you to determine whether Jordan and/or Emery are correct?
teQuestions.a: Check whether each expression was simplified according to the order of operations; if it was, the result is equivalent to the original equation, and if not, it is not.

teQuestions.q: Rewrite y = (1/3)(x - 1/2)^2 - 3/4 in the form y = ax^2 + bx + c.
How would you summarize the steps needed to rewrite the vertex form of the quadratic function in the form y = ax^2 + bx + c?
teQuestions.a: Square the binomial, distribute the coefficient, and then combine like terms.

teQuestions.q: Casey rewrote y = 2(x - 4)^2 + 5 as 2(x + 1)^2 = 2(x^2 + 2x + 1) = 2x^2 + 4x + 2. Is Casey correct? Explain.
teQuestions.a: No; Casey added 5 inside the parentheses. Expand first, then distribute the 2, then add like terms: y = 2x^2 - 16x + 37.

modelDiscuss.caution: The opener is the vertex-form-to-standard-form expansion (Example 1's derivation, cut), not the vertex formula the quiz needs; keep it to ten minutes and skip the early-finishers fractions. Bridge to Example 2 with the corrected y = 2x^2 - 16x + 37: its vertex is still (4, 5), and h = -b/(2a) = 16/4 = 4 gives it back, which is why the formula works. IXL 8GN (multiply polynomials) is the prerequisite for the expansion.

modelDiscuss.source: 2024 TE page 76B (Step 1, Explore; this lesson's opener is Critique & Explain)
modelDiscuss.situation: Martell wrote an equation in factored form, y = (x + 8)(x - 2), to represent a quadratic function. Kimberly wrote the equation y = x^2 + 6x - 16, and Takeisha wrote the equation y = (x + 3)^2 - 25. The graph is an upward parabola with vertex (-3, -25), x-intercepts -8 and 2, and y-intercept -16.
studentPrompts: A. Reason: Do all three equations represent the same function? If not, whose is different? Explain algebraically. (Yes: (x + 8)(x - 2) and (x + 3)^2 - 25 both simplify to x^2 + 6x - 16.)
B. How else could you determine if all three equations represent the same function? (Graph the three equations on the same plane.)
C. What information can Martell's form help you find that is more difficult to find using Kimberly's or Takeisha's form? (Where the graph crosses the x-axis.)

teQuestions.q: What key features from the graph relate to the students' equations?
teQuestions.a: The x-intercepts -8 and 2 from Martell's equation; the y-intercept -16 from Kimberly's; the vertex (-3, -25) from Takeisha's.

teQuestions.q: What strategy could you use to compare all three equations?
teQuestions.a: Write all equations in the same form: multiply out Martell's and Takeisha's binomials to get standard form.

teQuestions.q: What method can you use to verify that the graphs of the students' equations are the same?
teQuestions.a: Graphing calculator, table.

teQuestions.q: Write three different forms of a quadratic equation with x-intercepts of -6 and 4.
Why is it useful to write quadratic equations in different forms?
teQuestions.a: Each form can be used to identify certain key features of the graph of a function.

teQuestions.q: Whose form of the equation is most useful for finding the vertex? The y-intercept? The x-intercepts?
teQuestions.a: Takeisha's; Kimberly's; Martell's.

modelDiscuss.caution: Spend the opener on part C: Martell's factored form shows the x-intercepts -8 and 2, the bridge to the Zero Product Property (Example 3) and to y = a(x - p)(x - q) (Example 6). Part A's expanding is 2-2 review; two minutes. The early-finishers question (x-intercepts -6 and 4) is Example 6 with a = 1, a good preview. The TE spells the name both Martell and Martel.

modelDiscuss.situation: A class plays "Solve It, You're Out." Each student holds a card with an integer from -5 to 5; when an equation is shown, any student whose card is a solution is eliminated. Five students remain: Mercedes -3, Steve 0, Aubrey 1, Fatima 3, Elijah -2.
studentPrompts: A. The next equation presented was x^2 = 9. Which student(s) was eliminated? Explain. (Mercedes and Fatima: (-3)^2 = 9 and 3^2 = 9.)
B. Construct Arguments: in the next round, the equation presented was x^2 = -4. Is Elijah eliminated? Why or why not? (No: (-2)^2 = 4, not -4.)

C. What is true about solutions to x^2 = a when a is a positive number? When a is a negative number? What about when a = 0? (a > 0: two solutions, the square root of a and its opposite; a = 0: one solution, 0; a < 0: no real-number solutions.)

teQuestions.q: How can you tell whether someone should be eliminated from the game?
teQuestions.a: His or her card will contain a solution to the equation.

teQuestions.q: Explain how you can identify the number of solutions to the equation x^2 = a when a > 0 without calculating.
teQuestions.a: For any positive nonzero number there are two square roots, a positive and a negative one, so the equation has 2 solutions.

teQuestions.q: What equations of the form x^2 = a are needed to eliminate Steve, Aubrey, and Elijah?
teQuestions.a: x^2 = 0 eliminates Steve, x^2 = 1 eliminates Aubrey, and x^2 = 4 eliminates Elijah.

teQuestions.q: Are there any values for a for which nobody would be eliminated from the game?
teQuestions.a: Yes; when a is not equal to 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, or 25.

teQuestions.q: What values of a will eliminate only one person?
teQuestions.a: Considering the entire deck of Solve It! cards, only a = 0.

teQuestions.q: Steve thought that he was a sure winner because he could not be eliminated. Is he correct? Explain. If not, write an equation of the form x^2 = a that would eliminate Steve.
teQuestions.a: No; the equation x^2 = 0 would eliminate him.

modelDiscuss.caution: The opener leads to Example 1 (x^2 = a negative number), which is cut. Use part B and part C only, as the bridge to the packet's concept box (i is the square root of -1, i^2 = -1), five minutes at most, then go straight to Example 3. The Do Now stays the assigned IXL skill (5VV or VZ8), never this game.

modelDiscuss.situation: Hana and Enrique used different methods to solve the equation x^2 - 6x + 9 = 16. Hana subtracts 16, factors x^2 - 6x - 7 = (x - 7)(x + 1) = 0 and gets 7 and -1. Enrique writes (x - 3)^2 = 16, says 'I can square 4 or -4 to get 16', and gets x - 3 = 4 or x - 3 = -4, so 7 and -1.
studentPrompts: A. Does Hana's method work? If her method is valid, explain the reasoning she used. If her method is not valid, explain why not.
B. Does Enrique's method work? If his method is valid, explain the reasoning he used. If his method is not valid, explain why not.

C. Use Structure: Can you use either Hana's or Enrique's method to solve the equation x^2 + 10x + 25 = 3? Explain. (Enrique's: the left side is (x + 5)^2 and 3 is not a perfect square, so the solutions are irrational and factoring will not find them.)

teQuestions.q: How do the results of each student's work compare?
teQuestions.a: They both get the same answer.

teQuestions.q: How do the solution methods compare?
teQuestions.a: They both factored; however, Hana began by transforming the equation into the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0, and Enrique began by transforming the equation into the form (x - p)^2 = q.

teQuestions.q: How is the equation in Part C different?
teQuestions.a: There is not a way to factor it and set the factored expression equal to a perfect square.

teQuestions.q: Solve the equation in Part C. Whose solution method did you use? How do the solutions compare?
teQuestions.a: x = -5 +/- sqrt 3; Enrique's method; 3 is not a perfect square, so the solutions are irrational.

teQuestions.q: Do you think there are other methods for solving quadratic equations?
teQuestions.a: Yes. The left side of the quadratic equation in the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 can be graphed as a parabola. The real solutions can be seen as x-intercepts.

teQuestions.when: Habits of Mind, Make Sense and Persevere
teQuestions.q: Why does Hana set her two factors equal to zero, while Enrique sets his factors equal to 4 and -4?
teQuestions.a: Hana applies the Zero Product Property, while Enrique recognizes perfect squares on both sides of the equation and so uses square roots to solve.

modelDiscuss.caution: The opener's equations are already perfect square trinomials (Example 1 and quiz item 1 territory); nothing in it adds (b/2)^2. Use Part C as the bridge: ask what Enrique would do if the left side were x^2 + 10x with no 25, which is the key-idea box on page 1 and then Example 3. Do not let it run past 10 minutes on a brief lesson.

modelDiscuss.situation: You can complete the square to solve the general quadratic equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0 and derive the Quadratic Formula. The eight steps of the derivation are shown, from ax^2 + bx + c = 0 to x = (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac))/(2a).
studentPrompts: A. Construct Arguments: Justify each step in this general solution. (Subtract c; divide by a; add (b/2a)^2 to complete the square; factor and simplify; common denominator; take the square root of each side; subtract b/2a.)
B. What must be true of the value of b^2 - 4ac if the equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0 has two non-real solutions? If it has just one solution? (Negative for two non-real solutions; zero for one solution.)

teQuestions.q: Why might you want to complete the square on the general quadratic equation?
teQuestions.a: If you memorize the result of completing the square in general, it will be easier to complete the process when a, b, and c are replaced by numbers.

teQuestions.q: How would completing the square for an equation like 2x^2 + 7x + 6 = 0 help to understand how to solve ax^2 + bx + c = 0 for x?
teQuestions.a: Having a concrete model to follow makes it easier to apply the same process in an abstract situation.

teQuestions.q: Name values of a, b, and c that would result in two nonreal solutions.
teQuestions.a: 2, 4, 3: 4^2 - 4(2)(3) = -8 < 0. A negative b^2 - 4ac means taking +/- the square root of a negative number, which gives two nonreal solutions.

teQuestions.q: How did you determine what must be true about the value of b^2 - 4ac in order to have one solution or two nonreal solutions?
teQuestions.a: When b^2 - 4ac = 0, x equals -b/(2a), which yields one solution. When b^2 - 4ac < 0, the negative radicand implies nonreal solutions, and because of the +/- before the radical there are two of them.

teQuestions.q: Why is there a +/- sign in the second-to-last step of the derivation of the Quadratic Formula?
teQuestions.a: Both the negative square root and the positive square root give the same value when squared.

modelDiscuss.caution: Part A (justify eight algebra steps) is a full-period task and 2-5 Completing the Square is a brief lesson, so in the fast format show the derivation as a read-along and run only Part B: it is the discriminant idea of Example 3 and quiz items 3-5. The TE notes the digital board keeps (x + b/2a)^2 on the left of the square-root step; the student edition correctly shows x + b/2a.

modelDiscuss.source: 2024 TE page 105B, Step 1 Explore (Explore & Reason, powered by Desmos)
modelDiscuss.situation: Draw a rough sketch of a parabola and a line on the coordinate plane.
studentPrompts: A. Count the number of points of intersection between the two graphs. (Sample: 2 intersections.)

B. Sketch another parabola on a coordinate plane. Use a straightedge to investigate the different ways that a line and a parabola intersect. What conjectures can you make? (No points, one point where the line is tangent, or two points.)

C. Construct Arguments: How many different numbers of intersection points are possible between a quadratic function and a linear function? Justify that you have found all of the possibilities. (Zero, one or two.)

teQuestions.q: Describe the graph you sketched.
teQuestions.a: There are two equations graphed. One is a parabola and one is a line. The parabola and the line intersect in two places.

teQuestions.q: Would using a vertical line help you determine the different number of intersection points between a linear function and a quadratic function?
teQuestions.a: No; a vertical line is not a function.

teQuestions.q: If the line is of the form y = c, would it change the number of intersection points possible, when combined with the graph of a quadratic function?
teQuestions.a: No; a horizontal line could be drawn so as not to intersect with the parabola, to only intersect it at its vertex, or to intersect it at two points.

teQuestions.q: What method did you use to determine the possible number of intersection points?
teQuestions.a: Draw a parabola. Change the position of the straight edge so that it intersects the parabola at two points, at one point, or not at all.

teQuestions.q: Does changing the position of the parabola instead of the position of the line change the number of possible intersection points from 2, 1, or 0?
teQuestions.a: No; the number of possible intersection points is the same whether you move the line or the parabola.

teQuestions.q: What must be true about the equation for a horizontal line that has no points of intersection with the parabola of the equation y = x^2?
teQuestions.a: The equation must be of the form y = a, for a constant a < 0.

modelDiscuss.caution: The opener is Example 1's idea (0, 1 or 2 intersections), which the fast packet cuts; keep it to five minutes as the bridge to 'the solutions are the intersection points', which Example 3 needs, and to quiz item 1. The TE's printed Part C answer counts a line that 'bisects' the parabola as a one-point case; that line is vertical and not a function (the During question says so), so accept only a tangent line as the one-point case.

modelDiscuss.source: 2024 TE page 119B (Step 1, Explore & Reason, powered by Desmos)
modelDiscuss.situation: Consider functions of the form f(x) = x^n, where n is a positive integer.
studentPrompts: A. Graph f(x) = x^n for n = 1, 3, and 5. Look at the graphs in Quadrant I. As the exponent increases, what is happening to the graphs? Which quadrants do the graphs pass through? (Steeper; Quadrants I and III.)

B. Look for Relationships: now graph f(x) = x^n for n = 2, 4, and 6. What happens to these graphs in Quadrant I as the exponent increases? Which quadrants do the graphs pass through? (Steeper; Quadrants I and II.)

C. Write two equations in the form f(x) = x^n with graphs that you predict are in Quadrants I and II, and two with graphs in Quadrants I and III. Use graphing technology to test your predictions. (For example x^6, x^8; x^7, x^9.)

teQuestions.q: What do you know about the effect of exponents on negative and positive numbers?
teQuestions.a: A negative number raised to an even power gives a positive product; raised to an odd power, the product stays negative.

teQuestions.q: What general observation can you make about the graphs with exponents that are odd numbers?
teQuestions.a: They start at the bottom left, in Quadrant III, and move to the top right, in Quadrant I.

teQuestions.q: Graph f(x) = -x^n for n = 2, 3, 4, and 5. What happens to the graphs and the range of each function when -1 is the coefficient of x?
teQuestions.a: The graph is reflected across the x-axis. For n = 3 or 5 the range is unchanged; for n = 2 or 4 it changes from real numbers >= 0 to real numbers <= 0.

teQuestions.q: What generalizations can be made about how specific features of equations cause specific behaviors in the graphs?
teQuestions.a: For f(x) = x^n with an even exponent, points on both sides of the y-axis have positive y-values; with an odd exponent, points left of the y-axis have negative y-values and points right of it have positive y-values.

teQuestions.q: Compare the end behavior of f(x) = x^n for n = 1, 3, 5 with n = 2, 4, 10. Write a general statement comparing odd and even exponents.
teQuestions.a: When n is odd, the sign of the y-values differs as x approaches positive or negative infinity; when n is even, the sign is the same.

modelDiscuss.caution: The printed 'becomes steeper' describes the graphs outside -1 < x < 1; between 0 and 1 the higher powers are flatter (the TE notes this). The opener is Example 2's even/odd idea with leading coefficient 1, so it leads straight into the four-panel page; the early-finishers question (-x^n) is the negative-leading-coefficient half. Keep it to one Desmos round so Example 3 still gets its table.

dok3.label: Practice & Problem Solving 13, Reason (Example 1 DOK 3; item 11, Use Structure, is the other Example 1 DOK 3)
dok3.task: Polynomial function R is the difference of two degree-two polynomial functions. What are the possible degrees for R? Explain.
dok3.key: 2, 1, or 0. If the second-degree terms have the same coefficient they cancel, and the degree of the difference depends on the remaining first- or zero-degree terms. If every term cancels (the two functions are identical), R is the zero polynomial, which has no defined degree; so the degree goes down only when the difference is nonzero.
dok3.why: Students must build their own cases (different x^2 coefficients, then equal ones, then equal x terms too) and argue from like terms and coefficients; IXL items are DOK 1-2 and cannot stand in for it. It is the packet's exit question, with a sentence frame that reuses the language goal's words (like terms, coefficient, degree). Item 11 needs end behavior (3-1) and is the alternative. Quiz item 4 is also DOK 3, but it is the quiz item itself, so it cannot be the practised DOK 3.

modelDiscuss.source: 2024 TE page 127B, Step 1 Explore (Explore & Reason; the digital heading says Critique & Explain)
modelDiscuss.situation: Let S be the set of expressions that can be written as ax + b, where a and b are real numbers.
studentPrompts: A. Describe the Associative Property, Commutative Property, and the Distributive Property. Then explain the role of each in simplifying the sum (3x + 2) + (7x - 4). Identify the leading coefficient and the constant term in the result. (10x - 2: leading coefficient 10, constant term -2.)
B. Is the sum you found in part A a member of S? Explain. (Yes; it has the form ax + b.)
C. Construct Arguments: is the product of two expressions in S also a member of S? Explain why or produce a counterexample. (No; with a not 0 the product is quadratic, not ax + b.)

teQuestions.q: When have you used the Associative, Commutative, and Distributive Properties before?
teQuestions.a: To simplify numerical expressions and make mental math easier.

teQuestions.q: How does using the Distributive Property help you to simplify the expression?
teQuestions.a: After the Associative and Commutative Properties rearrange the terms, the Distributive Property rewrites 3x + 7x as (3 + 7)x.

teQuestions.q: Simplify (4x - 7) - 5x + 2x - 9 and (2x + 4 - 4x) + (-9x + 2 - 7 + 10x). What do you notice about each expression after it is simplified?
teQuestions.a: They are all in the form ax + b (x - 16 and -x - 1).

teQuestions.q: What generalization can you make about the effects of using addition and subtraction to simplify expressions?
teQuestions.a: Combining like terms only changes the coefficients; the variables and exponents do not change.

teQuestions.q: What have you learned about the Associative, Commutative, and Distributive Properties?
teQuestions.a: They can be used to simplify algebraic expressions.

teQuestions.q: Is the quotient of two expressions in S also a member of S? Explain why or produce a counterexample.
teQuestions.a: No. Counterexample: (x + 1) / (x + 2) cannot be written as ax + b. (The TE answer says that when the coefficients have no common factors the quotient has the form ax/(cx + d) + b/(cx + d); that holds when the divisor has an x term, but dividing by a nonzero constant, such as (2x + 4) / 2 = x + 2, stays in S.)

modelDiscuss.caution: The digital version of part A prints (3x - 2) + (7x - 4) while the student page prints (3x + 2) + (7x - 4); the TE answer (leading coefficient 10, constant term -2) fits the student page. Part A is Example 1's 'only the coefficient changes' idea and part C (the product leaves S) is the hook for Example 2; the Habits of Mind quotient question is closure (Example 3, cut), so keep it for early finishers only. The early-finisher expressions simplify to x - 16 and -x - 1 (computed; the TE prints no answers for them).

modelDiscuss.source: 2024 TE page 134B (Step 1, Explore & Reason; the digital heading says Critique & Explain)
modelDiscuss.situation: Pascal's Triangle, rows 1; 1 1; 1 2 1; 1 3 3 1; 1 4 6 4 1; 1 5 10 10 5 1. Each number is the sum of the two numbers diagonally above; if there is no second number, think of it as 0.
studentPrompts: A. Write the numbers in the next three rows. (1 6 15 20 15 6 1; 1 7 21 35 35 21 7 1; 1 8 28 56 70 56 28 8 1)
B. Look for Relationships: What other patterns do you see? (The numbers one from the left move up by 1 in each row.)
C. Find the sum of the numbers in each row of the triangle. Write a formula for the sum of the numbers in the nth row. (1, 2, 4, 8, ..., 256; 2^n)

teQuestions.q: What do you notice about the triangle?
teQuestions.a: There's one more number in each row than in the row above it.

teQuestions.q: Compare the rows of the triangle. What similarities and differences can you find?
teQuestions.a: The first and last number of a row is always 1; in every other row the center number is repeated.

teQuestions.q: How does the sum of the numbers in one row in the triangle compare to that of the row above it?
teQuestions.a: The sum of a row is double the sum of the row above it.

teQuestions.q: Look at the sums of the numbers in the diagonals of rows 0 through 8. Then write out the numbers for row 9. What do you notice? Do you think this will always be true?
teQuestions.a: The sums of the diagonals are the same numbers as the next row with an additional 1 at the end. This is always true.

teQuestions.q: How could you determine the first two numbers of a row using your patterns?
teQuestions.a: Call the first row row 0. The first number is 1 and the second is the row number.

teQuestions.q: How do you know the last two numbers of a row?
teQuestions.a: The rows are symmetric, so the last two numbers are the first two in reverse order.

quizFocus.source: a2_3-4_TE.tex Lesson Quiz; aga_24_a2_na_0304_lq.pdf when downloaded
quizFocus.what: Item 5: if x+2 is a factor of P(x) = 2x^3 + 5x^2 + 5x + 6, select the two factors that express P(x) as a product (A (x+2), B (2x^2 - x - 3), C (2x^2 - x + 3), D (2x^2 + x - 3), E (2x^2 + x + 3), F not a factor). Proposal for the 20 points: item 2 (finish Morgan's synthetic division by x - 2) and item 5 at 10 each, item 3 (verify the Remainder Theorem for x+2) the +5 bonus; the short form keeps the Savvas numbers 2, 3 and 5 and leaves off items 1 and 4.
quizFocus.answer: A, E: P(x) = (x+2)(2x^2 + x + 3); synthetic division with a = -2 gives the bottom row 2, 1, 3 | 0 (verify against the TE key on quiz day). Item 2: B (products 2, 6, 0, -8; quotient x^3 + 3x^2 - 4). Item 3: -23; -23; Yes.
needs: write the divisor x+2 as x-(-2), so a = -2 is the zero of the divisor (Example 5B). Corey's error in Reteach 2 is this one: 45 is P(2), the remainder is P(-2) = 13. Jettie's 149 in Do You Understand 2 is wrong too: the remainder for x+5 is P(-5) = -49
synthetic division: bring down, multiply by a, add; the bottom row except its last number gives the quotient, one degree lower than the dividend (Example 2; IXL D6D)
the last number of the bottom row is the remainder, and it equals P(a) (Remainder Theorem; Example 5 Methods 1 and 2 both give -21; IXL CHC)
remainder 0 means x - a is a factor, so P(x) = quotient times (x - a) (Factor Theorem; Example 5A; IXL VXE)
write 0 for a missing term of the dividend (Example 2's 0x, Example 5B's 0x^4, quiz item 4's missing x^3)

modelDiscuss.situation: Santiago tried factoring (x + 2) out of 3x^2 + 7x + 4. Using algebra tiles, he made a rectangle (three x^2 tiles, one x tile, and two rows of three x tiles and one 1 tile) with 2 unit tiles left over.
studentPrompts: A. Reason: Can you conclude whether (x + 2) is a factor of 3x^2 + 7x + 4? Explain your reasoning. (No: if x + 2 were a factor there would be no tiles outside the rectangle; here there is a remainder of 2.)
B. Write an expression for 3x^2 + 7x + 4 in terms of (x + 2). ((x + 2)(3x + 1) + 2)
C. Use algebra tiles to show 2x^2 + 7x + 6 divided by (x + 2). ((x + 2)(2x + 3), no tiles left over)

teQuestions.q: What is different about Santiago's arrangement of algebra tiles when compared to other arrangements you have seen?
teQuestions.a: There are 2 tiles that are not part of the arrangement.

teQuestions.q: Santiago arranged some of the algebra tiles to form a rectangle. What two factors do these tiles represent? What is their product?
How does this product compare to Santiago's original expression?
teQuestions.a: The constant term is 2 less than the constant term in Santiago's original expression.

teQuestions.q: Write an expression for 3x^2 + 14x + 18 in terms of (x + 3).
teQuestions.a: (x + 3)(3x + 5) + 3 (the TE prints the remainder as 3/(x + 3); the product form needs + 3).

teQuestions.q: How did you determine how to write the quotient of 2x^2 + 7x + 6 and x + 2?
teQuestions.a: Start with 2 x^2-tiles, 7 x-tiles and 6 unit tiles. Arranged into a rectangle with one x-tile and two 1-tiles along one side, the other side has 2 x-tiles and 3 1-tiles, with no tiles left over.

modelDiscuss.caution: The TE prints the answer to B (and to the early-finishers question) with the remainder as a fraction, (x + 2)(3x + 1) + 2/(x + 2); the product form is (x + 2)(3x + 1) + 2, so correct it on the board. The digital version of part A prints 3x^2 - 7x - 4; use the plus signs. quizFocus.source: a2_3-5_TE.tex Lesson Quiz (TE printed page 157A); aga_24_a2_na_0305_lq.pdf when downloaded
quizFocus.what: Item 1: Part A, all the zeros of f(x) = x^3 + 2x^2 - 3x; Part B, use the zeros to sketch the graph (Example 1 exactly). Item 5 (second graded item): find the zeros of f(x) = -x^3 - 2x^2 + 7x - 4 and pick the description of the graph at each zero (end behavior, sign between the zeros, tangent at the double zero), Examples 1 and 2 together. Item 4 (bonus): zeros and multiplicities of y = x^3 + 3x^2 + x + 3 from its graph.
quizFocus.answer: 1A: -3, 0, 1 (f = x(x + 3)(x - 1)); 1B: cubic crossing at -3, 0, 1, rising to the right, local max near (-1.9, 6.1), local min near (0.5, -0.9); 5: D (f = -(x - 1)^2(x + 4)); 4: B (-3, multiplicity 1; (x + 3)(x^2 + 1)) (verify against the TE key on quiz day)
needs: factor out the common x, then factor the quadratic (Example 1 step 1; IXL UB5 warm-up)
Zero-Product Property: each factor gives a zero (Example 1; IXL PVM)
sign of each factor on each interval, so the graph is above or below the x-axis between zeros (Example 1 sign table; IXL 8CQ)
odd multiplicity crosses, even multiplicity has a turning point at the x-axis (Example 2; IXL PVM, 8CQ)
item 5 starts in standard form: test a candidate zero (f(1) = 0), divide by x - 1 (synthetic division from 3-4), factor the quotient (the packet Practice; IXL NCY)
end behavior from the leading term -x^3 (quiz 5 choices A and B fail on it; IXL XMK, from 3-1)
item 4 (bonus) factors by grouping: x^2(x + 3) + (x + 3) = (x + 3)(x^2 + 1); one whiteboard round if the bonus stays (factor by grouping is not an assigned IXL skill here)

dok3.label: Practice & Problem Solving 30, Performance Task (DOK 3; the TE item analysis files it under Example 4)
dok3.task: Venetta opened several deli sandwich franchises in 2000. The profit P (in hundreds of dollars) of the franchises in t years (since the franchises opened) can be modeled by P(t) = t^3 + t^2 - 6t. Part A: sketch a graph of the function. Part B: based on the model, during what years did Venetta not make a profit? Part C: if the model is appropriate, predict the amount of profit Venetta will receive from her franchises in 2020.
dok3.key: Part A: P(t) = t(t + 3)(t - 2), zeros -3, 0, 2; for t >= 0 the graph dips below the axis between 0 and 2 (minimum near t = 1.1, P = -4.1) and then rises steeply (the TE graph shows t from 0 to 24 and P up to 16,000). Part B: the first two years (P(t) < 0 for 0 < t < 2). Part C: P(20) = 8000 + 400 - 120 = 8,280 hundred dollars = $828,000.
dok3.why: R3 asks for a DOK 3 tied to a kept Example, but the TE item analysis files all three DOK 3 items (25, 27, 30) under Example 4, which is cut; by the R3 exception Practice 30 is named as the lesson's DOK 3 and printed as the self-paced extension after Try It 1. modelDiscuss.source: 2024 TE page 150B (Step 1, Model & Discuss; Critique & Explain is the Realize alternative)
modelDiscuss.situation: Charlie's and Aisha's STEM club built a small rocket and launched it from a field. The rocket fell to the ground 5 s after it launched. Its height h, in feet, at time t seconds can be modeled by h(t) = at^2 + bt + c.
studentPrompts: A. How are the launch and landing times related to the modeling function? (h = 0 at both, so t = 0 and t = 5 solve 0 = at^2 + bt + c.)

B. What additional information about the rocket launch could you use to construct an accurate model for the rocket's height relative to the ground? (The height at another time, or the initial speed and gravitational acceleration.)

C. Construct Arguments: Charlie believes that h(t) = -16t^2 + 80t models the height of the rocket. Do you agree? Explain your reasoning and indicate the domain of this function. (Yes: it is 0 at 0 s and 5 s; domain 0 to 5.)

teQuestions.q: How would you describe the function that models the height of the rocket?
teQuestions.a: It is a quadratic function written in standard form. The variable t represents the time in seconds after the rocket was launched; the value of the function is the rocket's height t seconds after launch.

teQuestions.q: Why do you need additional information to construct an accurate model for the height of the rocket?
teQuestions.a: You need three points to write the equation of a parabola; the problem gives only two, the launch point and the landing point.

teQuestions.q: Another rocket was launched that fell to the ground 10 seconds after it was launched. How does the maximum height of this rocket compare to the first rocket?
teQuestions.a: The maximum height of this rocket is four times as high as that of the first rocket.

teQuestions.q: What information in the problem statement helps you determine the value of c in the model?
teQuestions.a: The rocket is launched from the ground, so when t = 0, h(0) = 0.

teQuestions.q: How can you determine the maximum height of the rocket in Charlie's model?
teQuestions.a: The maximum height occurs at t = 2.5, halfway between 0 and 5. Evaluate the function at t = 2.5.

teQuestions.q: In Charlie's function, what is the value of c? Why is this the correct value?
teQuestions.a: 0; the rocket is launched from the ground, a height of 0 ft.

modelDiscuss.caution: The TE's printed answer to C gives the domain as 'all x-values from 0 to 5'; the variable is t, so say 0 <= t <= 5. The opener is a quadratic, not a cubic: bridge to Example 1 by factoring Charlie's model as -16t(t - 5) and reading the launch and landing times off the factors (zero = factor). Keep it to one board round; the TE's early-finishers question is the stretch.

objectives.learning: I can describe how the graph of a cubic or quartic function is stretched, reflected, and translated from its parent function.
objectives.language: I can explain each change to a graph using the words parent function, leading coefficient, stretch, reflection, and translation.
objectives.essentialQuestion: How are symmetry and transformations represented in the graph and equation of a polynomial function?

quizFocus.source: a2_3-7_TE.tex Lesson Quiz (TE printed page 174A); aga_24_a2_na_0307_lq.pdf when downloaded
quizFocus.what: Item 2: identify the parent function of f(x) = -x^4 - 1 and list the transformations in order (A and B differ only by the order: translate then reflect vs reflect then translate; C and D name the cubic parent). Item 3 (second graded item): select all the true statements about how g(x) = 3x^3 + 6 differs from f(x) = x^3 (Example 3A and Try It 3 with new numbers). Item 4 (bonus): pick the equation of an upward quartic with labeled minimum (2, -3).
quizFocus.answer: 2: B (x^4; reflect over the x-axis, translate down 1 unit); 3: C, D; 4: D (f(x) = (x - 2)^4 - 3) (verify against the TE key on quiz day)
needs: parent function from the degree: x^3 (cubic) or x^4 (quartic) (Example 3 step 1; IXL KT8)
the leading coefficient multiplies every y-value: |a| > 1 stretches vertically (Example 3A; IXL KT8, RSN)
the added constant k translates vertically (Example 3A and Try It 3; IXL KT8)
a negative leading coefficient reflects over the x-axis and flips the end behavior (the packet Practice, TE Practice 18 and 8; IXL XMK warm-up, from 3-1)
order: stretch or reflect before the vertical translation, because -(x^4 - 1) = -x^4 + 1, not -x^4 - 1 (Example 3 TE question 'Is the order important?'; the Practice question)
item 4 (bonus) reads Example 3 backwards: the turning point (0, 0) moved to (h, k) = (2, -3); both ends up means a quartic with no reflection (Example 4, cut; IXL RSN)

dok3.task: Provide an example that demonstrates the following statement is not true. If the degree of a function is an even number, then the function is an even function.
dok3.key: TE sample: f(x) = 2x^4 + x^3 - 2 has even degree but is not even: f(-x) = 2(-x)^4 + (-x)^3 - 2 = 2x^4 - x^3 - 2, which is not equal to f(x) (the TE prints the second f(x) where f(-x) is meant). Also correct from Example 3: f(x) = (x - 2)^4 has degree 4, but its turning point is at (2, 0), so the graph is symmetric about x = 2, not the y-axis; f(1) = 1 and f(-1) = 81.

modelDiscuss.situation: Look at the polynomial graphs below: f(x) = x^2 (a parabola with vertex at the origin, both ends up) and g(x) = x^3 (through the origin, from lower left to upper right).
studentPrompts: A. Is the graph of f or g symmetric about the y-axis? Is the graph of f or g symmetric about the origin? Explain. (f is symmetric about the y-axis: its reflection across the y-axis is identical; g is symmetric about the origin: it is identical when rotated 180 degrees about the origin.)

B. Look for Relationships: graph more functions of the form y = x^n where n is a natural number. Which of these functions are symmetric about the origin? Which are symmetric about the y-axis? What conjectures can you make? (Even n: symmetric about the y-axis; odd n: symmetric about the origin.)

teQuestions.q: What do you notice about the two graphs?
teQuestions.a: f(x) is a parabola that opens upward; it is symmetric across the y-axis and has a minimum at the origin. g(x) is cubic; it passes through the origin and it is symmetric about the origin.

teQuestions.q: What does it mean for a graph to be symmetrical?
teQuestions.a: It has an axis of symmetry; the graph is reflected across a line. One part of the graph is the mirror image of the other part.

teQuestions.q: Graph the functions m(x) = x and h(x) = x^4. How does the symmetry of these graphs compare to the symmetry of f(x) and g(x)?
teQuestions.a: The graph of m(x) is symmetric about the origin, like the graph of g(x). The graph of h(x) is symmetric about the y-axis, like the graph of f(x).

teQuestions.q: What do you notice about the degree of the polynomial and the type of symmetry it has?
teQuestions.a: A polynomial with an even degree is symmetric about the y-axis. A polynomial with an odd degree is symmetric about the origin.

teQuestions.when: Habits of Mind, Look for Relationships
teQuestions.q: Do you notice any other patterns among the functions with even degree and the functions with odd degree?
teQuestions.a: Functions with an even degree always go the same direction when approaching positive and negative infinity, while odd functions always go opposite directions.

modelDiscuss.caution: The TE's After answer ('a polynomial with an even degree is symmetric about the y-axis') is true only for the power functions y = x^n on the screen, not for every polynomial; Practice 12 (the DOK 3 Extension) exists to break it. Say 'for y = x^n' on the board. The opener is about symmetry (Examples 1-2, cut); bridge to Example 3 in one board round: translate y = x^4 right 2 and ask whether it is still symmetric about the y-axis (no: the turning point moved to (2, 0)), then start Example 3 with what the leading coefficient and the constant do.

modelDiscuss.situation: Two rectangles both have an area of 144 square units: 72 by 2 and 24 by 6.
studentPrompts: A. Sketch as many other rectangles as you can that have the same area. Organize and record your data for the lengths and widths of the rectangles. (1 by 144, 3 by 48, 4 by 36, 8 by 18, 9 by 16, and 12 by 12)
B. Use Structure: considering rectangles with an area of 144 square units, what happens to the width of the rectangle as the length increases? (As the width increases, the length decreases.)

C. Examine at least five other pairs of rectangles, each pair sharing the same area. How would you describe the relationship between the lengths and widths? (In each pair, the lengths and widths are different by reciprocal factors.)

teQuestions.q: How many length-width combinations for a rectangle can be created from a given pair of factors?
teQuestions.a: Two; given the factors 2 and 3, a rectangle can have length 2 and width 3, or length 3 and width 2.

teQuestions.q: Do the lengths and widths always have to be integers?
teQuestions.a: No; a rectangle with a length of 5 units and a width of 28.8 units has an area of 144 square units.

teQuestions.q: Sketch as many rectangles as you can that have an area of 25 square units. Is the relationship between the lengths and widths the same as or different from the one for an area of 144 square units?
teQuestions.a: The same.

teQuestions.q: Can you write a general equation that models this situation?
teQuestions.a: xy = k

teQuestions.q: What would the equation look like solved for the dependent variable y?
teQuestions.a: y = k/x

teQuestions.q: How does the formula for the area of a rectangle make sense with the relationships you found?
teQuestions.a: Area is length times width, so any two factors could be the length and width and give the same product, the area.

modelDiscuss.caution: The opener is the constant product k = xy, which is Example 3 Step 1, so it bridges straight into the kept Example; keep it to the 'After' questions (xy = k, then y = k/x) and skip the sketching marathon in part A. The TE's part B answer swaps length and width (the prompt asks about the width as the length increases), and part C's answer 'different by reciprocal factors' is vague: say the product stays 144.

quizFocus.what: Item 3: the vertical and horizontal asymptotes of f(x) = (3-2x)/(4-3x). Choices A x = 4/3 and y = 2/3; B x = 2/3 and y = 4/3; C x = 3/4 and y = 2/3; D x = 3/2 and y = 4/3. Item 5 (also graded) is the same skill run backwards: which of four linear-over-linear functions has horizontal asymptote y = -3.
quizFocus.answer: Item 3: A (4 - 3x = 0 gives x = 4/3; equal degrees, so y = -2/-3 = 2/3). Item 5: C ((1-3x)/(2+x): -3/1). Item 1 bonus: C, p(x) = 2 - 1/(2x+4). (verify against the TE key on quiz day)

items.1: Match the graph (vertical asymptote x = -2, horizontal y = 2, right branch below y = 2) to p(x) = 2 +/- 1/(2x +/- 4). Answer C. DOK 1, F20. Example 1 writes functions in this k + a/(x-h) form (cut); Example 4 (asymptotes then a test point) answers it. Proposed +5 bonus.

modelDiscuss.source: 2024 TE page 189B, Step 1 Explore (Explore & Reason, powered by Desmos)
modelDiscuss.situation: Three functions: f(x) = x - 1, g(x) = (x - 1)/2 and h(x) = (x - 1)/(x - 2).
studentPrompts: A. Look for Relationships: graph each function. Determine which of the functions are linear. Find the y-intercept of each function and the slope, if appropriate. (f: linear, slope 1, y-intercept -1; g: linear, slope 1/2, y-intercept -1/2; h: not linear, y-intercept 1/2)
B. What is the effect on the graph of f when dividing x - 1 by 2? (Each y-value is half the previous y-value.)
C. What happens to the graph of h as x approaches 2? (From the left y goes to negative infinity; from the right, to positive infinity.)
D. Communicate Precisely: what is the effect on the graph of f(x) when dividing x - 1 by x - 2? (The graph is no longer linear.)

teQuestions.q: How are f(x), g(x), and h(x) similar? How are they different?
teQuestions.a: All three contain x - 1. g and h are fractions (rational expressions).

teQuestions.q: What are some strategies you can use to find the slope of the functions that are linear?
teQuestions.a: Graph and compute change in y over change in x for two points, or rewrite in slope-intercept form.

teQuestions.q: What are some strategies you can use to find the y-intercept?
teQuestions.a: Read where the graph crosses the y-axis, or evaluate f(0).

teQuestions.q: What do you notice about the end behavior of each function?
teQuestions.a: f and g go to infinity as x goes to infinity and to negative infinity as x goes to negative infinity. h approaches 1 as x goes to either infinity, and goes to positive or negative infinity as x approaches 2.

teQuestions.q: What do you notice about the graphs of functions that have a variable in the denominator?
teQuestions.a: They are not linear; they have asymptotes; their domain and range do not contain all real numbers (true for this launch example, not for every such function).

teQuestions.when: Habits of Mind, Look for Relationships
teQuestions.q: What similarities do you notice between the graph of h(x) = (x - 1)/(x - 2) and the graph of a reciprocal function?
teQuestions.a: Both have vertical and horizontal asymptotes and approach the horizontal asymptote as x goes to positive and negative infinity.

modelDiscuss.caution: h(x) = (x - 1)/(x - 2) is already Example 4's form: use part C (x approaching 2: the denominator is 0) as the bridge to Step 1 and the early-finishers answer (h approaches 1, the ratio 1/1) as the bridge to Step 2. Do not let the slope and intercept table in part A eat the period; f and g are review. The TE's 'After' answer overgeneralizes (not every function with a variable denominator has asymptotes, e.g. 1/(x^2+1) has no vertical one).

modelDiscuss.situation: The graph of the line y = x + 2, through (-2, 0) and (0, 2), on a grid from about -17.5 to 17.5 by -12.5 to 12.5.
studentPrompts: A. What is the domain of this function? (all real numbers)
B. Sketch a function that resembles the graph, but restrict its domain to exclude 2. (the line with an open circle at (2, 4))
C. Use Structure: Consider the function you have sketched. What kind of function might have a graph like this? Explain. (one whose denominator is zero when x = 2)

teQuestions.q: What do you notice about the graph of the function?
teQuestions.a: Sample: x-intercept -2; y-intercept 2; the function is linear.

teQuestions.q: Why is it important to know the domain of a function?
teQuestions.a: The domain needs to make sense for the scenario, and some values of x make the function undefined, so they cannot be in the domain.

teQuestions.q: Sketch the function y = -x + 4. What is the domain of the function?
teQuestions.a: All real numbers.

teQuestions.q: Sketch the graph of the function, excluding -4 from the domain. Describe the new graph created.
teQuestions.a: A line with a negative slope and an opening at x = -4; x-intercept 4, y-intercept 4.

teQuestions.q: How does the exclusion of an x-value in a function's domain due to an asymptote compare to the exclusion of an x-value at a single point?
teQuestions.a: An asymptote occurs where the denominator is zero and the numerator is not; the graph gets close to it but never touches. A single excluded point leaves a hole, with the function taking values close to the hole.

teQuestions.q: Does the graph of y = (2x + 6)/(x + 3) have a vertical asymptote at x = -3? Explain.
teQuestions.a: No; the function approaches (-3, 2) from both sides, so there is a hole at x = -3 instead of an asymptote.

modelDiscuss.caution: The TE's printed answer to C, y = (2x - 4)/(x - 2), simplifies to y = 2 with a hole at (2, 2); it does not give the line y = x + 2 drawn in B. Use y = (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2) instead (it simplifies to x + 2 with a hole at (2, 4)): that is Example 2's move in miniature, factor and divide out the common factor while the domain still leaves out 2, so the opener leads straight into the kept Example.

modelDiscuss.situation: Teo and Evander find 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/9 in their homework. Teo claims that a common denominator of the sum is 2 + 3 + 9 = 14; Evander claims that it is 2 x 3 x 9 = 54.
studentPrompts: A. Is either student correct? Explain why or why not. (Only Evander: a common denominator has each denominator as a factor.)
B. Find the sum, explaining the method you use. (17/18, rewriting each fraction with denominator 18.)

C. Construct Arguments: Timothy states that the quickest way to add any two fractions with unlike denominators is to multiply their denominators to find a common denominator. Do you agree? (No; the least common denominator may be faster.)

teQuestions.q: What do you notice about the expression in the homework exercise?
teQuestions.a: Three fractions are added. The numerator of each fraction is 1. Each fraction has a different denominator.

teQuestions.q: Compare common multiples and the least common multiple. How are they similar? How are they different?
teQuestions.a: The least common multiple is a common multiple. A group of numbers has many common multiples, but only one least common multiple.

teQuestions.q: Add 1/8 to the expression in the homework exercise. What are the least common denominator and the sum of the new expression?
Why would you want to use the least common multiple when writing fractions with a common denominator instead of any other common multiple?
teQuestions.a: The least common multiple gives you smaller numbers to compute.

teQuestions.q: How can there be more than one correct answer to this problem?
teQuestions.a: You can write the answer with different equivalent fractions: 17/18, 34/36, 51/54 and 68/72 are all equivalent.

teQuestions.when: Habits of Mind, Look for Relationships
teQuestions.q: For two fractions with denominators 10 and x, when is 10x the least common multiple? When is 10x NOT the least common multiple?
teQuestions.a: When x and 10 have no common factors (other than 1), 10x is the least common multiple; when they share a factor, it is not.

ixl.name: Solve a quadratic equation by factoring
Rational functions: asymptotes and excluded values

modelDiscuss.situation: Nicky and Tavon used different methods to solve the equation (1/2)x + 2/5 = 9/10. Nicky subtracts 2/5 (finding a common denominator: (1/2)x = 5/10) and gets x = 1. Tavon multiplies both sides by 10 to get 5x + 4 = 9, then x = 1.
studentPrompts: A. Explain the different strategies that Nicky and Tavon used and the advantages or disadvantages of each. (Tavon cleared the fractions by multiplying by 10, one extra step; Nicky kept the fractions and needed common denominators.)
B. Did Nicky use a correct method to solve the equation? Did Tavon? (Both methods are correct.)

C. Use Structure: Why might Tavon have chosen to multiply both sides of the equation by 10? Could he have used another number? Explain. (10 is the LCD; any common multiple works but means more reducing.)

teQuestions.q: What do you notice about the equation?
teQuestions.a: It is a linear equation; the coefficient of the x-term and the constants are fractions.

teQuestions.q: What strategy does Nicky use to solve the equation?
teQuestions.a: The same strategy as a linear equation with integers: subtract to isolate the variable term, then divide.

teQuestions.q: What strategy does Tavon use to solve the equation?
teQuestions.a: He multiplies each side by 10; because each side is multiplied by the same value, the result is an equivalent equation.

teQuestions.q: Solve (2/3)x - 4/5 = 1 1/5 using the methods that Nicky and Tavon use. Does each method give the same solution?
teQuestions.a: x = 3 both ways.

teQuestions.q: What do you notice if you rewrite each fraction with a denominator of 10?
teQuestions.a: The numerators are the numbers in Tavon's equation after multiplying by 10.

teQuestions.q: Substitute x = 1 into (1/2)x + 2/5 = 9/10 and 5x + 4 = 9. What does the result tell you?
teQuestions.a: Both are true: they are equivalent equations.

teQuestions.q: If Tavon multiplied each side by 100, would his answer have been 10 times as much? Explain.
teQuestions.a: No; multiplying each side by the same value does not change the solution.

modelDiscuss.caution: The TE prints Tavon's second line with the whole equation inside the parentheses, 10((1/2)x + 2/5 = 9/10); write it on the board as 10((1/2)x + 2/5) = 10(9/10). Tavon's move is exactly Example 1's (multiply both sides by the denominator), so the opener leads straight in. The opener's denominators are numbers, never 0; Example 4 is where multiplying by an expression like x - 2 can introduce an extraneous solution, so say that out loud when moving on.

needs: denominator of the exponent = index of the radical (which root), numerator = power (Example 2; concept summary; IXL 9TM)
recognise perfect powers: 243 = 3^5, 32 = 2^5, 27 = 3^3, 16 = 2^4, 625 = 5^4 (prereq; IXL EUH)
take the root first, then the power, so the numbers stay small: (fifth root of 243)^3 = 3^3 = 27 (Example 2B; IXL KJX)
get x^n alone first (divide by the coefficient, including a negative one: -4x^3 = 32 gives x^3 = -8), then raise both sides to the 1/n power (Example 5; IXL U42 for the root step)

an odd index gives one real root with the sign of the radicand (cube root of -8 = -2); an even index and a positive radicand give two real roots, +/- (x^4 = 625, x = +/-5), and a negative radicand gives none (Example 5B; quiz item 1)

modelDiscuss.situation: The graph of y = x^2 (a parabola with vertex at the origin) on a grid from about x = -5 to 5 and y = -5 to 15.
studentPrompts: A. Find all possible values of x or y so that the point is on the graph: (2, _), (3, _), (-3, _), (5, _), (_, 4), (_, -16), (_, 7), (_, 5). (4; 9; 9; 25; -2 and 2; no possible value; -sqrt 7 and sqrt 7; -sqrt 5 and sqrt 5)

B. Communicate Precisely: write a precise set of instructions that show how to find an approximate value of sqrt 13 using the graph. (Draw y = 13, then go straight down from where it meets the graph to the positive x-axis and read the value.)
C. Draw a graph of y = x^3. Use the graph to approximate the cube roots of 5, -5 and 8, and a solution to x^3 = 5, x^3 = -5 and x^3 = 8. (about 1.7; about -1.7; 2; about 1.7; about -1.7; 2)

teQuestions.q: What do you notice about the graph of y = x^2?
teQuestions.a: The graph is a parabola. All values of y are greater than or equal to zero.

teQuestions.q: What is true about the possible missing x-values compared to the possible missing y-values?
teQuestions.a: For a missing x-value there are 2 possible values (when y is positive); for a missing y-value there is only 1 possible value.

teQuestions.q: Draw a graph of y = x^4 and y = x^5 and use them to approximate values as in Part C. How do the numbers of x- and y-values compare to y = x^2 and y = x^3?
teQuestions.a: A positive y-value of y = x^4 has 2 x-values, like y = x^2. Each y-value of y = x^5 has 1 x-value, like y = x^3.

teQuestions.q: Can the instructions you created in Part B be used to approximate the cube root of a number?
teQuestions.a: Yes: find the point whose y-value is the number under the radical sign and read its x-value.

teQuestions.q: What do you notice about the answers in Part C?
teQuestions.a: The cube root of 5 equals the solution to x^3 = 5, the cube root of -5 the solution to x^3 = -5, and the cube root of 8 the solution to x^3 = 8.

teQuestions.when: Habits of Mind, Look for Relationships
teQuestions.q: How is sqrt 5 related to 5? How is the cube root of 5 related to 5? How do you think the fourth root of 5 is related to 5?
teQuestions.a: (sqrt 5)^2 = 5; (cube root of 5)^3 = 5; (fourth root of 5)^4 = 5.

modelDiscuss.caution: The TE's printed During answer says every missing x-value has two possibilities, but its own Part A lists (_, -16), which has none, and y = 0 has only one: say 'two for a positive y'. quizFocus.answer: Item 1: A, 21x^2 - 7x + 34. Item 5: D, 3x - 10 with domain x >= 4. Item 4: D, -1. (TE key, recomputed; verify against the TE key on quiz day.)
needs: composition: apply the inside function g, then the outside function f; (f o g)(x) = f(g(x)) (concept box)
substitute a whole expression for x, in parentheses, everywhere x appears, including a lone x (Example 5B's Watch line: the lone x becomes (4 - x); IXL EKJ)
read f(g(x)) as g first, then f: the inside function is applied first (concept box; Example 6; IXL RSP), because item 1's choice C is the reversed order

the domain of f o g takes two checks, x in the domain of g and g(x) in the domain of f: in Example 5A the outside square root sets the limit (2x - 5 >= -7, so x >= -1); in item 5 the inside function g(x) = sqrt(x - 4) does, so x >= 4 even though 3x - 10 simplifies to a line (the packet's concept box: check 1, x in the domain of g; check 2, g(x) in the domain of f; item 5 choice C is that trap)
add two functions by combining like terms, the + g(x) in item 1 (Example 1, cut; starred IXL QQD)

dok3.label: Practice & Problem Solving 16, Higher Order Thinking (Example 6 DOK 3; 32, Use Structure, is the other Example 6 DOK 3 and the packet's self-paced extension)
dok3.task: Suppose two functions, f(x) and g(x), are only defined by the ordered pairs listed below. f = (6,7), (5,2), (4,1), (10,8); g = (5,4), (3,6), (1,5), (2,10). Find the ordered pairs that comprise (f o g)(x).
dok3.key: (f o g)(x) = {(5,1), (3,7), (1,2), (2,8)}: g(5) = 4 and f(4) = 1; g(3) = 6 and f(6) = 7; g(1) = 5 and f(5) = 2; g(2) = 10 and f(10) = 8. Every output of g is an input of f, so the domain of f o g is {5, 3, 1, 2}, the domain of g. (TE key: {(5,1),(3,7),(1,2),(2,8)}.)
dok3.why: With no rule to substitute, students must use the meaning of composition (the output of the inside function becomes the input of the outside function) and see the domain of f o g as the inputs of g whose outputs f accepts; that is the concept box, quiz item 4's inside-out evaluation and quiz item 5's domain in one task. IXL is DOK 1-2 and cannot stand in for it. It is the packet's Exit question, with a Say it frame on the language-goal words (inside function, domain). Practice 32 (music store, $90 purchase: $72.25 with $5 off first, $71.50 with 15% off first) is Example 6's structural sibling and the self-paced extension.
